About Card Match
Card Match is a spatial working memory and visual pattern recall test. Face-down cards are arranged in a grid; you flip two cards at a time to find matching symbol pairs while minimizing total moves and elapsed time.
What Card Match Measures
This module measures immediate visual-spatial buffer capacity, spatial coordinate retention, and memory decay under interference. As more cards are revealed, earlier card locations compete with newer visual inputs in working memory.
How Scoring Works
Scores are calculated based on: (1) Total moves taken to clear the board, (2) Total completion time in seconds, and (3) Move efficiency (ideal moves / actual moves × 100%). Lower moves and faster times yield higher percentile rankings.
Difficulty Configurations
Beginner uses a 4×2 grid (4 pairs), Normal uses a 4×4 grid (8 pairs), and Hard/Expert uses up to a 6×6 grid (18 pairs) with tighter card flip timeouts and visual distractors.
Optimal Memory Strategies
Use a systematic spatial grid indexing strategy (e.g. scanning row-by-row) rather than random exploratory flips. Associate card symbols with spatial anchor landmarks (top-left, center, bottom-right) to reinforce recall.
Empirical Baseline Targets
On an 8-pair (4×4) grid, an average adult typically finishes within 14–18 moves in 20–30 seconds. Elite performers with strong spatial chunking clear 8 pairs in 10–12 moves in under 15 seconds.

Enhances visual and spatial memory retention under constraints.
Improves pattern recognition across 6 to 36 flippable targets.
Trains rapid cognitive filtering (matching both emojis AND border colors).
Increases short-term focus through positive and negative time incentives.

About the Chimp Test
The Chimp Test is a visuospatial working-memory challenge inspired by ape cognition studies. Numbers appear on a grid; after you tap 1, the rest hide and you must tap the blank cells in ascending order from memory.
What It Measures
Success depends on encoding spatial positions quickly, holding them after numbers vanish, and retrieving them without relying on leftover visual cues. Typical comfortable spans for adults often sit around 5–7 items; larger spans need strong chunking.
How a Round Works
A set of numbered cells appears. Memorize locations. Tap 1 to begin recall—remaining digits hide. Tap the empty cells in order 2, 3, 4… A wrong cell costs a life (depending on difficulty).
Difficulty Modes
Easier modes use fewer numbers, slower vanish timing, and more lives. Harder modes enlarge the grid, hide numbers faster, and leave less forgiveness. Professional play is about encoding under time pressure, not casual browsing.
Strategies That Help
Group numbers into shapes (triangle, L, diagonal). Rehearse a short path aloud. Do not stare at one cell—scan the whole set once, then lock a spatial story.
Score Meaning
Higher completed span (how many numbers you cleared) is better. Compare yourself across the same difficulty only—grid size changes the task.
Why Spatial Working Memory Matters
Visuospatial working memory supports navigation, diagram reading, and keeping track of several locations at once. When the numbers vanish, you experience the same pressure athletes and operators feel when a brief glance must become an action plan.
Training Without Overclaiming
Raising your chimp-test span shows you can encode and retrieve more spatial items under this exact rule set. That is valuable practice. It does not by itself prove higher general intelligence. Treat personal bests as skill metrics, not labels.

About Color Memory
Color Memory, based on the famous Stroop Effect, is an advanced cognitive training tool designed to challenge and enhance your ability to inhibit cognitive interference. This engaging test measures your brain's capacity to process color information while suppressing automatic reading responses, training selective attention and cognitive flexibility.
Understanding the Stroop Effect
The Stroop Effect demonstrates interference in reaction time when processing conflicting information. When you see the word 'RED' written in blue ink, your brain experiences conflict between the automatic reading response and the conscious color identification task. Color Memory trains you to overcome this interference, enhancing your cognitive control and selective attention abilities.
The Science Behind Color Memory
Research in cognitive psychology demonstrates that regular practice with Color Memory strengthens the neural pathways responsible for inhibitory control, improving your ability to focus attention and suppress automatic responses.

About This Test
About N-Back
N-Back is a continuous working-memory updating task. Letters appear in a stream; you respond when the current letter matches the one from N steps earlier.
What N Means
1-back: match the previous letter. 2-back: match the letter two trials ago. 3-back: three ago. Higher N forces a longer rolling buffer under time pressure.
Errors That Matter
Misses (no response on a true match) and false alarms (responding on a non-match) both hurt. Lives or accuracy metrics track both.
Difficulty Mapping
Beginner/Easy typically use 1-back. Normal/Hard use 2-back. Professional uses 3-back with faster timing and fewer lives.
Why People Train It
It stresses monitoring, updating, and interference control—core working-memory operations studied for decades.
Honest Transfer
Expect better N-Back performance with practice. Broad IQ claims are debated; treat this as targeted working-memory exercise.
Updating Under Load
Each new letter must enter the buffer while an older one drops off. That updating operation—not raw storage alone—is why N-Back feels uniquely taxing compared with static digit span.
Signal Detection Mindset
Think in hits, misses, and false alarms. A high hit count with many false alarms is not mastery. Aim for balanced sensitivity: catch real matches without triggering on lookalikes.
Program Design Tips
Climb N only after accuracy is stable. Jumping to 3-back while still chaotic on 2-back trains guessing. Log accuracy % beside hit count so progress is honest.

About Multiple Object Tracking
Multiple Object Tracking (MOT) asks you to follow several target dots among identical distractors while they move, then select the targets when motion stops.
Attentional Demand
You maintain an attentional set, survive path crossings without identity swaps, and resist distractors that pass nearby.
Round Structure
Targets flash, all dots move, then you click the original targets. Crowding and crossings create most errors.
Difficulty
More targets, higher speed, shorter mark time, and denser fields increase load.
Use Cases
Sports vision, driving awareness drills, and esports situational attention—transfer still needs real-task practice.
Scoring Mindset
Prioritize percent of targets recovered before raising set size.
Identity Over Location Snapshots
Beginners remember a screenshot of positions at one moment, then fail when objects move. Experts maintain continuous trajectories. Narrate silently: top-left target drifting down, etc.
Crowding and Capacity
Attention capacity for MOT is limited. Adding targets is not linear difficulty—it often collapses abruptly. Respect that cliff; train just below it.
Sports Parallel
Keeping tabs on teammates and opponents resembles MOT, but sport also adds meaning and prediction. Use MOT as a attention gym, then apply scanning in the real activity.
What This Test Trains
Enhances dynamic visual attention and peripheral vision.
Improves ability to focus on multiple moving targets simultaneously.
Builds cognitive endurance through sustained tracking periods.
Directly translates to real-world skills like driving or playing sports.

About Verbal Memory
Verbal Memory tests recognition of words across a continuous stream. Each word is either new in the session or a repeat. You must judge SEEN vs NEW without a word list to review.
Cognitive Demand
You update a growing set of encountered words, resist proactive interference, and decide under time pressure on harder modes. That stresses verbal working memory and familiarity monitoring.
How Gameplay Works
Words appear one at a time. Tap SEEN if it already appeared this run; tap NEW otherwise. Strikes accumulate on mistakes until the run ends.
Difficulty Changes
Harder modes enlarge the word bank (repeats are rarer and easier to miss), tighten timing, and reduce allowed strikes. Visually similar words increase false familiarity.
What Scores Mean
Higher words survived before strike-out is better. Compare runs on the same difficulty. Late-game confusion is normal as interference builds.
Real-World Link
Similar skills support reading comprehension, following conversations, and noticing when information is truly new versus repeated.
Familiarity vs Recollection
Late in a run you may feel a word is familiar without remembering the moment you saw it. That fuzzy familiarity drives false SEEN responses. Slowing half a second to ask when you saw it cuts those errors.
Interference Is the Real Boss
As the encountered set grows, older words compete with new ones. That is proactive interference—the same reason long study lists feel muddy. Short breaks between runs help more than forcing another exhausted attempt.
Practical Study Link
The same monitoring skill helps when rereading notes: noticing what is genuinely new versus repeated. Pair this game with real retrieval practice (flashcards, closed-book recall) for academic goals.

About Choice Reaction Time
Choice RT measures how quickly you select the correct option among multiple alternatives after a stimulus appears—closer to multi-button real life than simple one-button RT.

Several boxes wait. After a random delay, one lights. Click only that box. Early clicks and wrong boxes are errors.

Random foreperiods stop pure anticipation so you measure decision-plus-motor latency, not prediction.

Beginner uses fewer choices; harder modes add boxes, tighten timing, and may show decoy highlights on Professional.

Average RT in ms on correct hits—lower is better. Best RT stores your best average for that difficulty.

Hover readiness without twitching. Choice errors explode when you guess early.

The winning pattern is perceive → select → move. Starting the mouse motion before the light appears creates early-click faults and messy averages.

About Go/No-Go
Go/No-Go measures response inhibition: press quickly on Go cues and withhold on No-Go cues. An ~80% Go rate builds a press habit so No-Go trials become the real challenge.
What It Measures
Speeded motor readiness plus inhibitory control—the ability to cancel a prepared action when the cue says stop.
Trial Anatomy
Green (Go): press Space/tap ASAP. Red (No-Go): do nothing. Misses and false alarms both reduce score.
Difficulty
Harder modes add trials and shorten stimulus windows / gaps so decisions stack rapidly.
Score Reading
Count correct trials (Go hits + successful withholds). Also watch Go reaction time—fast but reckless play spikes false alarms.
Where It Shows Up
Impulse control under speed pressure matters in driving, sports, and fast UI work—this is a lab-style drill, not a full clinical battery.
Prepotent Responses
When most trials say Go, your motor system prepares to press by default. No-Go trials measure whether you can cancel that preparation in time—the essence of response inhibition.
Speed Accuracy Tradeoff
Chasing the lowest Go RT usually raises false alarms. Set a personal rule: never press unless the green is clearly confirmed. Slightly slower Go hits with clean withholds produce better overall scores.
Transfer Expectations
Improved inhibition on this task can support better stop-signal habits in games and driving drills, but real-world impulse control also depends on sleep, stress, and context.

About Time Perception
This test measures how accurately you can produce a target interval (for example 5 seconds) using only your internal sense of time—no on-screen countdown while you hold.
What It Measures
Time production depends on attention, arousal, and your internal clock. Stress and distraction commonly make people release early; boredom can stretch subjective time.
How a Trial Works
Read the target duration. Press and hold. Release when you believe the interval has elapsed. Score is absolute error in milliseconds—lower is better.
Difficulty
Harder modes demand tighter error margins and may add visual distractors that warp attention away from timing.
Interpreting Results
Average people often miss by roughly 10–20% on uncued intervals. Track average error across rounds, not a single lucky trial.
Training Use
Useful for musicians, athletes, streamers, and anyone who needs better interval feel—pair it with real metronome practice for music.
Attention Gates the Clock
When attention drifts to a distraction, subjective time often compresses and you release early. When you hyper-focus on the hold itself, you may overshoot. Aim for a steady secondary task like silent counting, not empty waiting.
Environment Controls
Compare sessions only when caffeine, sleep, and noise are similar. Arousal changes timing more than people expect. Keep the same hand posture and do not watch other clocks in the room.
Building Interval Sense
Alternate uncued production trials with occasional checked practice using a metronome offline. The game measures uncued skill; the metronome teaches a stable beat you can later reproduce without looking.

Click numbers in ascending order (or descending on Hard). The timer runs until the grid is finished. Wrong clicks flash; keep going for the correct target.

Faster clears usually mean wider useful field of view and less tunnel scanning. Soft focus on the center beats row-by-row reading.
Score
Completion time in ms—lower is better. Store bests per difficulty.

Prefer several clean clears over one panicked Professional attempt.

The goal is to widen the area from which you can pick out a digit without moving your eyes to every cell. Soft focus is a skill; it feels vague at first and then suddenly clicks.

About Precision Click
Small targets appear briefly; you must click them accurately. It measures pointer control, visual acquisition, and click discipline.

Raw CPS means little if misses explode. High accuracy with solid pace is the training goal.

Targets spawn → click before timeout → targets shrink as you score → session clock ends the run.
